[Tornadoes](/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") and [waterspouts](/wiki/Waterspout "Waterspout") may lift up animals into the air and deposit them miles away.

French physicist [André-Marie Ampère](/wiki/Andr%C3%A9-Marie_Amp%C3%A8re "André-Marie Ampère") (1775–1836) was among the first scientists to take accounts of raining animals. Addressing the Society of Natural Science, Ampère suggested that at times frogs and toads roam the countryside in large numbers, and that violent winds could pick them up and carry them great distances.[[3]](#cite_note-Ampère-3)

After a reported rain of fish in Singapore in 1861, French naturalist [Francis de Laporte de Castelnau](/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Louis_de_la_Porte,_comte_de_Castelnau "François Louis de la Porte, comte de Castelnau") speculated that a migration of [walking catfish](/wiki/Walking_catfish "Walking catfish") had taken place, dragging themselves over land from one puddle to another, following the rain.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

The likeliest explanation for many of the supposed cases is that there is no falling happening at all and the animals are driven along by winds or a deluge of some sort.[[9]](#cite_note-Nobel_2014-9) This explanation accounts for the prevalence of reports that just a single species or type of animal raining from the sky. In several occurrences within two weeks of October, 1987, people in three towns of [Gloucestershire](/wiki/Gloucestershire "Gloucestershire"), [England](/wiki/England "England") named [Stroud](/wiki/Stroud "Stroud"), [Cirencester](/wiki/Cirencester "Cirencester"), and [Cheltenham](/wiki/Cheltenham "Cheltenham") reported heavy rain fall that also brought down dozens of tiny pink frogs. The [Yellow River](/wiki/Yellow_River "Yellow River") gets most of its water from Gansu, flowing straight through Lanzhou. The area around Wuwei is part of [Shiyang River Basin](/w/index.php?title=Shiyang_River_Basin&action=edit&redlink=1 "Shiyang River Basin (page does not exist)").[[25]](#cite_note-26)

The landscape in Gansu is very mountainous in the south and flat in the north. The mountains in the south are part of the [Qilian Mountains](/wiki/Qilian_Mountains "Qilian Mountains"), while the far western [Altyn-Tagh](/wiki/Altyn-Tagh "Altyn-Tagh") contains the province's highest point, at 5,830 metres (19,130 ft).
